chapters.title: Listening to a teacher vs. seeing one

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: This afternoon I was talking with somebody, and I said, oh, I need to show you something in a book. And they immediately opened up the book to the page they had found before. And as they read that page, I was like — oh my gosh, that's the key, that's the secret.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So we're going to go on a little field trip right now, and then come back to what we started with. There's a big difference between sitting in a class and listening to a teacher, and then having a direct perception of a teacher.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Let me say it one more time so you can maybe feel the difference. It's really easy to come to Casa Tartuk. It's really easy to turn on your Zoom and sit down and say, yes, I'm going to learn something tonight. I'm going to listen to a teacher. And then I'm going to do something with that teaching — hopefully you're not just here to waste your time. And you can listen and listen and listen and never have a direct experience of that change.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So there's a capacity to listen, a capacity to think, a capacity to do all the work we did last night — we were logically working those pieces out. And then there's a direct perception of it. Was there a moment last night that touched you, where you felt like there was something you embodied differently about yourself? I saw it in some of you. I saw the movement. It was different than just listening. There was some kind of direct perception happening that was embodied within you. You were having an experience. Yes, listening is an experience too. But there's a distinction between someone who listens and the activation of it. Those are two very different things. And so when you’re listening to the teacher, there’s a difference between listening and thinking you have a teacher, and having a direct perception of a teacher.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So, Gina, slide number two.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: There's a difference between a projector that works and one that you're just thinking it works, right? Okay, so let's make this easy.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: This is a brachiosaurus. This is a dinosaur. One of the big dinosaurs. Has anyone seen a live dinosaur? No. Only the bones, right? Where I grew up, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, they had — weirdly — the largest collection of dinosaur bones in the world, at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History. Tons of dinosaur bones. I would go there like twice a year as a kid. I loved it. And I always wanted to meet a dinosaur. I still have dreams about meeting dinosaurs — sometimes they're like velociraptors and they try to eat me, and sometimes they're elegant, gentle creatures, like these giant brachiosauruses. So, no one's had a direct experience of a dinosaur, right?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Next video — the short one, the one that's in slide three. The buildup is incredible. So we have the picture of a dinosaur. Very beautiful. Very nice. I'd put this in my house.
{short clip from Jurassic Park (1993), when they see the dinosaurs for the first time}
“Alan, this species of variformin has been extinct since the Cretaceous period. I mean, this thing isn't like this thing. … What? What is it? Look! It's a dinosaur.”

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: We spent a lot of time on that. But understand the difference between looking at the picture and then seeing it for real — the difference between listening to a teacher and then having a direct perception of a teacher. There's a big, big difference. When you watch a teacher doing teacher things — and I'm not talking about them saying stuff in class, but watching the teacher be a teacher, and then having a direct perception of them teaching — it's a completely different experience. It's completely different in the level of learning and integration, and the capacity for a teacher to change you.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Where does it come from? Does it come from the teacher? No. This thing — You, and the changed person, the teacher who's changing you. It's you and seeing the teacher. You experiencing the change. So when we talk about narratives, or changing belief systems, we're not talking about "change the story and therefore your world is going to be different." The seed has to be there for that to happen. And if you've ever had an experience watching a teacher — it's like when the actor goes like this, and she's like, what? That's how it feels, because something deep inside you changes in that moment.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So you work on that for a little. And the text I read this afternoon — Je Tsongkapa says something important, from The Three Principal Paths. He says: you're absolutely going to have to go and learn from a teacher. Just reading Dharma books is never going to work. There's never been a single person in the history of the world who gained their spiritual goals without a teacher, just by relying on the books of the Dharma. And it'll never happen in the future either.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And I read this not as just Dharma books, but as listening to a class too. There's a deep difference between someone who listens and someone who — what word are you going to use? — integrates it. It's not just applying, it's integrating.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So when you have a teacher, you have to think. You have to spend a lot of time being like, is this the right person for me? And I'm not selling Buddhism. I'm not saying you have to be a Buddhist. I want you to find your teacher. I want you to find the person, or persons — because it can be more than one — where you can have that direct perception of change, where you become a different person. Meaning the seed opens up. The cascade of seeds opening up is you. You open up as a different you. Who are those people, or that person, for you?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: It's a personal thing. And you have to spend time with them, and see what they're doing, and ask yourself: is this the right place for me? If I'm going to open my heart and open up my spiritual real estate to someone who can change me — who's ringing the doorbell? Who are you going to let ring your doorbell? Who are you going to let in?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And you have to be very careful. Who are the people around them? Who are the students? Do you see the students changing? What happens when a student misbehaves? Because every community has people that act stupid — because we're all practitioners. If we were perfect already, we wouldn't need teachers. Teachers may not be perfect yet either. Teachers can make mistakes. How you view those mistakes is a different question. But if a teacher makes a mistake and then they don't own it — or if students are making mistakes or misbehaving — how the community handles those misbehaviors says a lot about the teacher or the teachings.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And then there's a big separation between the teacher and the teachings. The teachings could be pure and the teacher is an idiot. Or the teacher is unethical. And that's why it's so important — the way that people can misinterpret things so easily. What does something look like to somebody else, whether or not they're actually misbehaving?

chapters.title: The Vinaya, and how things look to others

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Last year, a student asked me for a walk-and-talk. I was like, well, look, I've got five minutes between this and that. And we walked. And I walked up to my room — I needed to get something. I got to the door, and I was like: wow, what would this look like to somebody else?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: A student, 20-plus years younger than me, wearing a shirt that's a little — you know — a little extra skin. We were in the middle of a conversation. I was like, if we continue this, we walk into my room — where nothing's going to happen — but then we walk out together, and someone's down at the end of the hall, and they see us walking out of my hotel room. What are they going to think? What could they think? There's a million stories they can create, and 99.9% of them are not true.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And I was like, oh, this is why the Vinaya says you can't have someone in your room who you would be attracted to, by yourself. This is for ordained people. But it also applies to normal people, especially in a professional context. Look, go have all the relations you want. I don't care. I'm not policing anyone's life. But as a director of V Houses, if I'm at a V Houses event and I walk out of my room with a woman who's 20 years younger than I am, wearing half her clothes — what is everyone going to think? And then everyone's going to be like, oh, well, the director can do that, so then what kind of organization is this?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So I was like, oh, that's why all those Vinaya things actually make a lot of sense. That's why I see my teacher, who has attendants who walk with him. So he's up there having a private meeting with a student, and the attendant is like ten steps behind. So everyone knows, oh, that's a private meeting. There's no — as we say in English — hanky-panky going on. People can see it and say, ah, look, he's having a meeting, this is private.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: You see? What does it look like, and what could be interpreted? In any kind of community — for some reason, people judge spiritual communities more harshly than any other community. There's a higher standard. Sorry, it's just the way the world is. The way it looks to someone — we have to be very careful of that. And then, as teachers, we have to be very careful.
